claim: The olfactory bulb (OB) receives dense GABAergic and cholinergic long-range projections from basal forebrain (BF) nuclei.
source: The olfactory bulb (OB), the first relay for odor processing in the brain, receives dense GABAergic and cholinergic long-range projections from basal forebrain (BF) nuclei that provide information about the internal state and behavioral context of the animal.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is consistent with established knowledge in the field.

claim: BF projections to the OB provide information about the internal state and behavioral context of the animal.
source: The olfactory bulb (OB), the first relay for odor processing in the brain, receives dense GABAergic and cholinergic long-range projections from basal forebrain (BF) nuclei that provide information about the internal state and behavioral context of the animal.
evidence: This is a statement about the functional role of BF projections, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: GABAergic BF inputs potently blocked PG cells firing except in a minority of calretinin-expressing cells.
source: GABAergic BF inputs potently blocked PG cells firing except in a minority of calretinin-expressing cells in which GABA release elicited spiking.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including loose cell-attached recordings and whole-cell recordings.

claim: In a minority of calretinin-expressing PG cells, GABA release from BF inputs elicited spiking.
source: GABAergic BF inputs potently blocked PG cells firing except in a minority of calretinin-expressing cells in which GABA release elicited spiking.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing excitatory GABAergic responses in some CR+ cells.

claim: Cholinergic projections from BF excited a previously overlooked PG cell subtype via synaptic activation of M1 muscarinic receptors.
source: Parallel cholinergic projections excited a previously overlooked PG cell subtype via synaptic activation of M1 muscarinic receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using optogenetic stimulation and pharmacological blockade with M1 receptor antagonists.

claim: Low-frequency stimulation of cholinergic axons drove persistent firing in type 2.3 PG cells.
source: Low-frequency stimulation of the cholinergic axons drove persistent firing in these PG cells, thereby increasing tonic inhibition in principal neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing sustained firing in response to 0.5 Hz photostimulation.

claim: Low-frequency stimulation of cholinergic axons increased tonic inhibition in principal neurons.
source: Low-frequency stimulation of the cholinergic axons drove persistent firing in these PG cells, thereby increasing tonic inhibition in principal neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased IPSC frequency in tufted cells following cholinergic stimulation.

claim: BF inputs can orchestrate synaptic inhibition in OB glomeruli using multiple, potentially independent, inhibitory or excitatory target-specific pathways.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that modality-specific BF inputs can orchestrate synaptic inhibition in OB glomeruli using multiple, potentially independent, inhibitory or excitatory target-specific pathways.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Basal forebrain nuclei innervate many regions of the brain including the entire neocortex, hippocampus, amygdala, thalamus, and hypothalamus.
source: Basal forebrain (BF) nuclei innervate many regions of the brain, including the entire neocortex, hippocampus, amygdala, thalamus, and hypothalamus, with diffuse long-range projections releasing GABA, ACh, and, more rarely, glutamate.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field and citations.

claim: BF projections release GABA, ACh, and more rarely, glutamate.

claim: BF projections modulate sensory perception, metabolic functions, brain states, and cognitive functions including attention, arousal, memory, and learning.
source: They modulate multiple synaptic, cellular, and network processes at a variety of temporal and spatial scales, thereby regulating sensory perception, metabolic functions such as food intake, brain states, and important cognitive functions, including attention, arousal, memory or learning (Ballinger et al., 2016; Picciotto et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cholinergic and GABAergic BF projections to the OB principally originate in the nucleus of the horizontal limb of the diagonal band of Broca (HDB) and in the magnocellular preoptic nucleus (MCPO).

claim: GABA release inhibits spiking through GABAA receptors in type 2.3 PG cells.
source: GABA release inhibits spiking through GABAA receptors, whereas ACh release activates mAChRs and produces a long-lasting excitation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings with gabazine.

claim: ACh release activates mAChRs and produces a long-lasting excitation in type 2.3 PG cells.
source: GABA release inhibits spiking through GABAA receptors, whereas ACh release activates mAChRs and produces a long-lasting excitation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings with muscarinic antagonists.

claim: In previous work, no BF-evoked muscarinic EPSC was detected in whole-cell recordings from various PG cell subtypes in dlx5/6 mice.
source: In our previous report, we did not detect any BF-evoked muscarinic EPSC in whole-cell (WC) recordings from various PG cell subtypes in dlx5/6 mice (Sanz Diez et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings from the same author.

claim: In dlx5/6 mice, a single photostimulation evoked a biphasic response initiated by an outward IPSC followed by a slow-rising inward current in 7/12 cells.
source: In dlx5/6 mice, a single photostimulation evoked a biphasic response initiated by an outward IPSC followed by a slow-rising inward current in 7/12 cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In ChAT mice, BF axons photostimulation induced a slow inward EPSC in 5/5 cells.
source: In ChAT mice, BF axons photostimulation induced a slow inward EPSC in 5/5 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings.

claim: Photo-evoked muscarinic EPSCs recorded at negative holding potentials were small and often at the limit of detection (max 10 pA, mean 5 ± 3 pA).
source: In both transgenic lines, photo-evoked muscarinic EPSCs recorded at negative holding potentials (from –30 to –60 mV) were small and often at the limit of detection (max 10 pA, mean 5 ± 3 pA, data obtained in ChAT and dlx5/6 mice pooled together).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings.

claim: Photo-evoked EPSPs did not exceed 5 mV (mean 3.1 ± 1.1 mV, two cells in ChAT mice and three cells in dlx5/6 mice).
source: In current-clamp, at membrane potential close to the resting potential, photo-evoked excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs did not exceed 5 mV (mean 3.1 ± 1.1 mV, two cells in ChAT mice and three cells in dlx5/6 mice)) (Figure 5A and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 5A and D.

claim: Muscarinic EPSC/EPSP ran down in few minutes.
source: Unfortunately, muscarinic EPSC/EPSP ran down in few minutes, precluding any further characterization.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental recordings.

claim: All ACh-responsive PG cells had the typical morphology of PG cells with small, ovoid, or round soma, no apparent axon, and thin dendrites projecting within a single glomerulus.
source: All had the typical morphology of PG cells. Their soma was small, ovoid, or round, with no apparent axon. Thin dendrites projected within a single glomerulus (Figure 5B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 5B and E.

claim: The average electrical membrane resistance of ACh-responsive PG cells was 1061 ± 524 MΩ.
source: On average, their electrical membrane resistance was 1061 ± 524 MΩ.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings.

claim: ACh-responsive PG cells all fired regularly at up to 100 Hz with overshooting action potentials in response to depolarizing current steps.
source: They all fired regularly at up to 100 Hz with overshooting action potentials in response to depolarizing current steps (Figure 5B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and E.

claim: ACh-responsive PG cells had a prolonged response to a single electrical stimulation of the ONs consisting of a barrage of fast EPSCs lasting several hundreds of ms (average 1760 ± 927 ms, n = 10).
source: Another striking hallmark of these PG cells was their prolonged response to a single electrical stimulation of the ONs. ON-evoked response consisted of a barrage of fast EPSCs lasting several hundreds of ms (average 1760 ± 927 ms, n = 10) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: ON-evoked responses in ACh-responsive PG cells had an onset latency >2 ms (average 3.14 ± 0.66 ms).
source: Evoked responses had an onset latency >2 ms (average 3.14 ± 0.66 ms) as typically seen in pluri-synaptic ON-evoked responses of type 2 PG cells (Sanz Diez et al., 2019; Najac et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous literature.

claim: In dlx5/6 mice, photo-evoked BF IPSCs in ACh-responsive cells were particularly slow (average decay time constant 162 ± 55 ms, range 69–258 ms, n = 16).
source: Finally, in dlx5/6 mice, photo-evoked BF IPSCs (amplitude range 10–186 pA, mean 62 ± 40 pA) were particularly slow (average decay time constant 162 ± 55 ms, range 69–258 ms, n = 16) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The intrinsic and synaptic properties unambiguously identify type 2.3 PG cells as the principal and perhaps unique synaptic target of BF cholinergic axons among PG cells.
source: Together, these intrinsic and synaptic properties unambiguously identify type 2.3 PG cells as the principal and perhaps unique synaptic target of BF cholinergic axons among PG cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Photostimulation of BF fibers did not evoke any response in type 1 PG cells (n = 4), type 2.1 PG cells (n = 21), and type 2.2 PG cells (n = 17) in ChAT mice.
source: Photostimulation of the BF fibers did not evoke any response in type 1 PG cells (n = 4), type 2.1 PG cells (n = 21), and type 2.2 PG cells (n = 17).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings in ChAT mice.

claim: Only one PG cell in ChAT mice responded with a fast IPSC, possibly reflecting unspecific expression of ChR2 in BF GABAergic neurons.
source: Only one PG cell, which could not be unambiguously classified, responded with a fast IPSC, a rare event that possibly reflected unspecific expression of ChR2 in BF GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This is an observation with a speculative interpretation.

claim: BF cholinergic axons innervating the glomerular layer of the OB have a unique and selective synaptic target among PG cells and do not release GABA.
source: Together, these results indicate that BF cholinergic axons innervating the glomerular layer of the OB have a unique and selective synaptic target among PG cells and do not release GABA.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: M1 receptors are widely expressed in the OB.
source: M1 receptors are widely expressed in the OB (Le Jeune et al., 1995) and their blockage impairs olfactory-evoked fear learning (Ross et al., 2019), making them a likely candidate.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Blockage of M1 receptors impairs olfactory-evoked fear learning.
source: M1 receptors are widely expressed in the OB (Le Jeune et al., 1995) and their blockage impairs olfactory-evoked fear learning (Ross et al., 2019), making them a likely candidate.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Pirenzepine (1–2 µM) fully blocked the excitation evoked by light stimulation of the BF fibers in six cells and reduced its strength in four cells.
source: Pirenzepine fully blocked the excitation evoked by light stimulation of the BF fibers in six cells and reduced its strength in four cells (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Post-stimulation spike frequency was reduced fourfold by pirenzepine (control: 10 ± 3.4 Hz; pirenzepine: 2.6 ± 3.3 Hz, p<0.0001).
source: On average, post-stimulation spike frequency was reduced fourfold by pirenzepine (control: 10 ± 3.4 Hz; pirenzepine: 2.6 ± 3.3 Hz, p<0.0001, data from ChAT and dlx5/6 mice pooled together, Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: M1 receptors mediate the muscarinic excitation of type 2.3 PG cells.
source: These results support the idea that M1 receptors mediate the muscarinic excitation of type 2.3 PG cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pirenzepine experiments.

claim: Hybridization signals for Chrm1 mRNA were found around DAPI-stained nuclei in all layers of the OB.
source: Hybridization signals were found around DAPI-stained nuclei in all layers of the OB (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence in situ hybridization shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The Chrm1 signal was particularly strong in granule cells.
source: The signal was particularly strong in granule cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D), consistent with previous functional data demonstrating that M1 mAChRs potentiate the excitability of granule cells (Pressler et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-D and citations to previous literature.

claim: M1 mAChRs potentiate the excitability of granule cells.
source: The signal was particularly strong in granule cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D), consistent with previous functional data demonstrating that M1 mAChRs potentiate the excitability of granule cells (Pressler et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: All granule cells recorded in ChAT mice in the LCA mode were silent and remained silent during low-frequency photostimulations of the cholinergic fibers (n = 17).
source: However, all the granule cells recorded in this study in ChAT mice in the LCA mode were silent and remained silent during the low-frequency photostimulations of the cholinergic fibers (n = 17, not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from loose cell-attached recordings.

claim: Most cells around glomeruli expressed the mRNA transcript of Chrm1.
source: However, most cells around glomeruli expressed the mRNA transcript of Chrm1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence in situ hybridization.

claim: The Chrm1 transcript was expressed in 85% of CR-positive cells (n = 372 cells counted) and 94% of TH-positive cells (n = 181 cells).
source: Moreover, ISH combined with immunodetection of CR or tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), two commonly used markers of nonoverlapping juxtaglomerular cell types, revealed that the Chrm1 transcript was expressed in 85% of the CR-positive (n = 372 cells counted) and 94% of the TH-positive cells (n = 181 cells) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Multiple cell types in the glomerular layer express M1 receptors.
source: These results thus suggest that multiple cell types in the glomerular layer express M1 receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in situ hybridization data.

claim: M1 receptors classically suppress the M current, a slow voltage-activated potassium current mediated by KCNQ2/3 potassium channels.
source: M1 receptors classically suppress the M current, a slow voltage-activated potassium current mediated by KCNQ2/3 potassium channels and active at resting membrane potential (Brown and Passmore, 2009; Suh and Hille, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: KCNQ2 subunits are strongly expressed in PG cells.
source: KCNQ2 subunits are strongly expressed in PG cells (Cooper et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: XE-991 increased baseline spike frequency in all type 2.3 PG cells tested (n = 14).
source: XE-991 had two noticeable effects in type 2.3 PG cells recorded in LCA. First, it increased baseline spike frequency in all the cells tested (n = 14, eight in dlx5/6 mice, six in ChAT mice, Figure 6C–E), suggesting that M-channels are indeed open at rest in type 2.3 PG cells and hyperpolarize their membrane potential.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: M-channels are open at rest in type 2.3 PG cells and hyperpolarize their membrane potential.
source: XE-991 had two noticeable effects in type 2.3 PG cells recorded in LCA. First, it increased baseline spike frequency in all the cells tested (n = 14, eight in dlx5/6 mice, six in ChAT mice, Figure 6C–E), suggesting that M-channels are indeed open at rest in type 2.3 PG cells and hyperpolarize their membrane potential.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effect of XE-991 on baseline firing.

claim: XE-991 reduced the strength of BF-induced excitation in type 2.3 PG cells.
source: Second, although XE-991 did not fully block photo-evoked muscarinic excitation in most cells (Figure 6C and F), it reduced the strength of BF-induced excitation (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C-F.

claim: Activation of M1 mAChRs depolarizes type 2.3 PG cells by blocking a potassium M current.
source: Overall, these data support the hypothesis that activation of M1 mAChRs depolarizes type 2.3 PG cells by blocking a potassium M current.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the XE-991 experiments and established knowledge about M1 receptor signaling.

claim: Photostimulation of cholinergic axons did not evoke any response in mitral cells (n = 17).
source: Photostimulation of the cholinergic axons significantly increased IPSCs frequency in eTCs (n = 9) and s/mTCs (n = 10) (Figure 7), whereas no response was found in mitral cells (n = 17).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Baseline IPSCs frequency was on average smaller in s/mTC (7.0 ± 5.1 Hz) compared to eTC (15.7 ± 10 Hz, p=0.0285).
source: Baseline IPSCs frequency greatly varied across cells and was on average smaller in s/mTC (7.0 ± 5.1 Hz) compared to eTC (15.7 ± 10 Hz, p=0.0285, t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from voltage-clamp recordings.

claim: Low-frequency photostimulation led to a rapid and persistent increase in IPSCs frequency in 8/10 eTC and 10/23 s/mTC.
source: Thus, low-frequency photostimulation led to a rapid and persistent increase in IPSCs frequency in 8/10 eTC and 10/23 s/mTC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from voltage-clamp recordings.

claim: The increase in IPSCs frequency was blocked or reduced when the experiment was repeated in the presence of 2 µM pirenzepine.
source: This response was blocked (n = 8) or reduced (n = 3) when the experiment was repeated in the presence of 2 µM pirenzepine (Figure 7C and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and E.

claim: A single photostimulation transiently increased IPSCs frequency in eTC (n = 9) and s/mTC (n = 8).
source: A single photostimulation also transiently increased IPSCs frequency in eTC (n = 9) and s/mTC (n = 8) (Figure 7B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and D.

claim: Type 2.3 PG cells release GABA onto tufted cells following their excitation by muscarinic activation.
source: Together, these results suggest that type 2.3 PG cells release GABA onto tufted cells following their excitation by muscarinic activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings showing increased IPSCs in tufted cells.

claim: A second group of cells in dlx5/6 mice responded to optogenetic stimulation of BF axons with a transient block of spiking (n = 45/383, 12% of cells tested).
source: Besides type 2.3 PG cells described above, a second group of cells in dlx5/6 mice responded to the optogenetic stimulation of the BF axons with a transient block of spiking immediately after the photostimulation (n = 45/383, 12% of the cells tested) (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Cells with only inhibitory responses did not show evidence of parallel cholinergic excitation.
source: However, unlike type 2.3 PG cells, they did not show any evidence of parallel cholinergic excitation.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental recordings.

claim: Basal firing frequency in cells with only inhibitory responses was on average higher than in type 2.3 PG cells (mean 7.8 ± 5.6 Hz, n = 21, p=0.00058).
source: In these cells, basal firing frequency was, on average, higher than in type 2.3 PG cells (mean 7.8 ± 5.6 Hz, n = 21, p=0.00058, Mann–Whitney rank-sum test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from loose cell-attached recordings.

claim: BF-induced inhibition persisted in the presence of NBQX, D-AP5, and mecamylamine (n = 9) and was blocked by gabazine (n = 7).
source: In the latter, BF-induced inhibition persisted in the presence of the blockers (n = 9) and was blocked by gabazine (Figure 8B, n = 7), suggesting that it was caused by a direct GABAergic BF input.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Cells with inhibitory responses had properties consistent with those of type 2.2 PG cells.
source: Altogether, these properties match well with those of type 2.2 PG cells (Najac et al., 2015). This suggests that type 2.2 PG cells only receive an inhibitory GABAergic input from the BF.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison with previously characterized cell types.

claim: Photo-evoked BF inputs elicited a single spike or doublet in a small number of cells in dlx5/6 mice (n = 29/383, 7% of cells tested).
source: Finally, photo-evoked BF inputs elicited a single spike (Figure 9A) or, more rarely, a doublet (Figure 9C) in a small number of cells in dlx5/6 mice (n = 29/383, 7% of the cells tested).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A and 9C.

claim: Excitatory responses were not seen in ChAT mice.
source: These excitatory responses were not seen in ChAT mice, persisted in the presence of NBQX, D-AP5, and mecamylamine (n = 6), and were blocked by gabazine (n = 4, Figure 9B and D), suggesting that they were caused by a direct excitatory GABAergic input.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental recordings.

claim: Excitatory responses persisted in the presence of NBQX, D-AP5, and mecamylamine (n = 6) and were blocked by gabazine (n = 4).
source: These excitatory responses were not seen in ChAT mice, persisted in the presence of NBQX, D-AP5, and mecamylamine (n = 6), and were blocked by gabazine (n = 4, Figure 9B and D), suggesting that they were caused by a direct excitatory GABAergic input.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B and D.

claim: Most cells with an excitatory response (26/29) had no or little (<1 Hz) spontaneous firing activity.
source: It would not be surprising if GABA was depolarizing in CR-expressing PG cells that retain many properties of newborn immature neurons (Benito et al., 2018). Consistent with this hypothesis, most of the cells with an excitatory response (26/29) had no or little (<1 Hz) spontaneous firing activity, similar to CR + PG cells (Benito et al., 2018; Fogli Iseppe et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous literature.

claim: Photo-evoked action potentials occurred within a short delay after the flash in 15/29 cells (average spike timing 13.4 ± 9.9 ms).
source: However, photo-evoked action potentials occurred within a short delay after the flash, as expected for synaptically driven spikes, in only 15/29 cells (average spike timing 13.4 ± 9.9 ms, Figure 9A and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A and E.

claim: In cells with delayed spikes, the average delay was longer (329 ± 191 ms) and more variable (n = 14).
source: In the other cells, the average delay was longer (329 ± 191 ms) and more variable (n = 14, Figure 9C and E), suggesting that distinct mechanisms drive the two types of response.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C and E.

claim: The photo-evoked BF synaptic input evoked a small but detectable gabazine-sensitive capacitive current that was inward in 14/15 cells responding with early spikes.
source: Strikingly, the photo-evoked BF synaptic input evoked a small but detectable gabazine-sensitive capacitive current that was inward in 14/15 cells responding with early spikes (Figure 9A, B, and E), whereas it was outward in all the cells responding with delayed spikes (Figure 9C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A, B, C, and E.

claim: The capacitive current was outward in all cells responding with delayed spikes.
source: Strikingly, the photo-evoked BF synaptic input evoked a small but detectable gabazine-sensitive capacitive current that was inward in 14/15 cells responding with early spikes (Figure 9A, B, and E), whereas it was outward in all the cells responding with delayed spikes (Figure 9C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C-E.

claim: A depolarizing GABAergic input directly triggered early spikes.
source: Thus, a likely explanation of the data is that a depolarizing GABAergic input directly triggered early spikes, whereas delayed spikes could be induced by rebound depolarization following a hyperpolarizing GABAergic IPSP, as often seen in CR + PG cells (Benito et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the direction of the capacitive current and citations to previous literature.

claim: Delayed spikes could be induced by rebound depolarization following a hyperpolarizing GABAergic IPSP.
source: Thus, a likely explanation of the data is that a depolarizing GABAergic input directly triggered early spikes, whereas delayed spikes could be induced by rebound depolarization following a hyperpolarizing GABAergic IPSP, as often seen in CR + PG cells (Benito et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the direction of the capacitive current and citations to previous literature.

claim: Eight cells responding with early action potentials had properties consistent with those of CR + PG cells.
source: Eight cells responding with early action potentials in the cell-attached mode (average timing 20 ± 19 ms) were subsequently characterized in the WC configuration. All of them had properties consistent with those of CR + PG cells, that is, a large input resistance (6 ± 3.1 GΩ), a characteristic voltage response to depolarizing current steps, and a large and fast photo-evoked BF IPSC (amplitude range 133–1300 pA, mean 370 ± 139 pA; weighted decay time constant 7.7 ± 3.6 ms) (Figure 9G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9G.

claim: The BF GABAergic input is depolarizing in as much as half of the CR-expressing type 2.1 PG cells.
source: Altogether, this analysis suggests that the BF GABAergic input is depolarizing in as much as half of the CR-expressing type 2.1 PG cells that may have an elevated chloride reversal potential, more depolarized than the membrane potential.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of capacitive currents in cells with and without spikes.

claim: The BF GABAergic input drives spiking in only a minority of CR-expressing type 2.1 PG cells.
source: However, this input drives spiking in only a minority of them.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proportion of cells showing spike responses.

claim: OB-projecting BF neurons have diverse impacts on PG cells.
source: This study shows that OB-projecting BF neurons have diverse impacts on PG cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: GABAergic inputs potently block the discharge of type 2.2 and type 2.3 PG cells with a target-specific time course.
source: GABAergic inputs potently block the discharge of type 2.2 and type 2.3 PG cells with a target-specific time course.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: GABA release is excitatory and triggers action potentials in a fraction of type 2.1 PG cells.
source: In contrast, GABA release is excitatory and eventually triggers action potentials in a fraction of type 2.1 PG cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: BF cholinergic fibers strongly and exclusively excite type 2.3 PG cells.
source: Data also reveal that BF cholinergic fibers strongly and exclusively excite type 2.3 PG cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Intraglomerular inhibition of principal neurons mediated by PG cells can be modulated in various ways by multiple BF pathways.
source: Thus, intraglomerular inhibition of principal neurons mediated by PG cells can be modulated in various ways by multiple BF pathways that potentially regulate olfactory processing in a context and behavior-specific manner.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.
